steps.scene: You're invited to a pub lunch. You know you'll have to drive that evening.

question.prompt: What should you do about alcohol?

options.text: Have a hot meal alongside your drinks
Don't drink any alcohol at all
Stick to one type of drink

question.explanation: Alcohol stays in your body for hours. If you're driving later in the day, the safe amount is none.

steps.title: It takes the judgement first
steps.body: Alcohol slows reactions, blunts your sense of danger and reduces your ability to judge speed — while making you feel more confident.

question.prompt: You've had a drink or two. What's the effect behind the wheel?

options.text: Your ability to judge speed is reduced
Your reactions get faster
You drive worse but you know you're doing it

question.explanation: The cruel part is the confidence: judgement falls while your belief in your own driving rises.

steps.title: Drowsy means stop
steps.body: If you begin to feel drowsy, stop and rest as soon as you safely can. Plan rest stops into any long journey before you set off.

question.prompt: You start to feel drowsy at the wheel. What do you do?

options.text: Open the window and press on more slowly
Stop and rest as soon as possible
Turn the heater up to stay comfortable

question.explanation: Fresh air and radios buy you seconds, not alertness. The only fix for tiredness is stopping.

steps.scene: You're an hour into a motorway journey and your eyes are getting heavy. The hard shoulder is right there.

options.text: Pull onto the hard shoulder for a nap
Leave at the next exit or services and rest
Speed up to finish the journey sooner

question.explanation: The hard shoulder is for emergencies only. Leave at the next exit or services, then rest properly.

steps.wrongBelief: Medicine you can buy without a prescription can't affect your driving.

question.prompt: You've taken a medicine that makes you drowsy. What now?

options.text: Drive only on quiet roads
Avoid driving and check with your doctor
Drive as normal — it's not a prescription drug

question.explanation: Drowsiness is drowsiness whatever caused it. Read the label, and ask your doctor if you're unsure.

steps.repairNote: Cough and cold remedies can make you drowsy too. Check the label before driving, and ask your doctor if unsure.

steps.title: Glasses are not optional
steps.body: If you need glasses or lenses to read a number plate at the required distance, you MUST wear them every time you drive.

question.prompt: When must you wear the glasses you need to read a number plate?

options.text: Whenever you're driving
Only at night and in bad weather
Whenever you think it's necessary

question.explanation: It's a legal requirement, not a judgement call — and tinted lenses make night driving harder still.

steps.scene: You're unsure of your route. The map is on the passenger seat and the next junction is coming up fast.

options.text: Glance at the map between mirror checks
Stop somewhere safe and check it there
Take the junction and work it out after

question.explanation: Reading a map at the wheel is a serious distraction. Nothing may take your attention off the road.
